The Eastern chestnut mouse Pseudomys gracilicaudatus exhibits life-history traits characteristic of a relatively slow-paced small mammal. Females give birth to litters of approximately three pups [N_R_i = litters of approximately three pups], and available data from related species suggest that breeding females may produce as many as three litters per year [F_R_i = three litters per year], yielding a substantial annual reproductive output for a murid rodent of this body size. Neonates are remarkably small at parturition, with a wet weight at birth of just 3.8 grams [Wwb = 3.8 grams], a value that underscores their altricial developmental state and complete dependency on maternal care during the initial postnatal period.

Gestation in Pseudomys gracilicaudatus proceeds relatively quickly, with embryonic development requiring 27 days [tg = 27 days] under typical maternal body temperatures of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This interval is comparable to that documented in other small-bodied Australian murids and reflects the accelerated pace of organogenesis characteristic of altricial eutherians. Following parturition, the suckling juveniles remain entirely dependent on milk for their nutritional requirements. Weaning, marking the cessation of lactation and the transition to solid food, occurs at 24 days after birth [tx = 24 days after birth], again at the same core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively brief suckling period is consistent with the species' small neonatal mass and rapid early growth trajectory.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs well after the attainment of nutritional independence. Field studies and captive records indicate that puberty is reached at 145 days after birth [tp = 145 days after birth] under thermoneutral conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This protracted interval between weaning and the onset of gonadal activity is likely linked to the energetic demands of achieving adult body size before reproductive effort can be initiated. Indeed, ultimate wet weight for adult females averages 69.3 grams [Wwi = 69.3 grams], a modest mass that places the species among the smaller members of the genus Pseudomys. Adult males attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 90.5 grams [Wwi = 90.5 grams], indicating pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size.

Longevity records for Pseudomys gracilicaudatus, extrapolated from data on the congener Pseudomys australis, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under controlled captive conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan is notably extended for a rodent of its body mass, exceeding predictions based on allometric scaling relationships for small mammals. The species' comparatively slow life-history pace is further reflected in its reproductive schedule; following the attainment of maturity, females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate consistent with producing 3 litters per year with 3 pups per litter, as described previously. This combination of small litter size, extended longevity, and delayed maturation aligns with a bet-hedging strategy typical of mammals inhabiting unpredictable environments.

Habitat preferences of Pseudomys gracilicaudatus centre on dense, structurally complex heathlands and wet sclerophyll forests along the eastern coast of Australia, where they construct burrow systems that provide thermal buffering against environmental extremes. Within these stable microclimates, the species maintains a core body temperature near 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], which is the thermal reference point for all metabolic and developmental measurements reported here. Diet consists primarily of seeds, fungi, and invertebrates, with seasonal shifts reflecting resource availability. Population densities fluctuate markedly in response to rainfall patterns, and during favorable periods, breeding can occur throughout the year. The species' ecological flexibility and relatively low reproductive output per event make it a useful model for understanding life-history evolution in small mammals under variable resource regimes, particularly in comparison to other members of the Pseudomys genus that occupy more arid zones.
